title: The Thiele Machine: A Computational Model with Explicit Structural Cost
description:
I didn't invent a machine. I found one. That is my conviction. The Thiele Machine is an abstract model of computation, a machine the way Turing's is, and this work is an argument made with it about which distinctions an account of computation should preserve. It is not a CPU, an instruction set, or category theory; the VM and hardware here are one build of the model, kept as witnesses.

A computation gives you an answer. What did it establish on the way there? Which distinctions did it keep? What did it cost to establish them? Certification is one point I could pin down. The machine carries structural state, a cost ledger, and rules for particular events. Its proofs show exactly what specified observations lose. A full encoding can preserve those distinctions; the question is which ones our models should keep.

The formal development includes accounting laws for systems satisfying A2, pricing adequacy for designated events, ledger uniqueness for a fixed schedule, observation adequacy, and exact conditions for descent from instruction traces to reachable-state simulations. A finite family of unit event floors can share one charge. Retaining history makes a deterministic step injective without changing its observed transition. On a finite state space that escape is closed: a certificate no step revokes can only be switched on by a step that merges states, so pricing merges, as Landauer's principle does in the worst case over what the machine might hold, yields A2; the heat comes from uncertainty about the state, and a known state owes none. Priced per halving, switching k states on beside m certified ones costs at least log2((m+k)/m), and on finite hardware the events that must be priced are exactly the merges, with every permanent-record write among them. The same bound holds in bits of Shannon entropy, and a finite fragment of the VM is such a machine, run by the VM at exactly its merge price; the full VM, by design, prices only the merge that certifies. An exact price for certification cannot be computed from a window in which a certifying step and a non-certifying one look alike, and the VM has such a pair. Three results carry the weight of the structural question: every deterministic machine can carry the record axis, as itself plus a latch on an event it reaches; on the VM the record cannot be recovered from the named windows; and on finite hardware a step that writes a permanent record merges states, so pricing merges prices the write. That a permanent record is a latch on one event is close to definitional. Which event is latched, the pointer question, is open. Those are mathematical answers with explicit premises.

The repository contains the Coq kernel, an extracted OCaml runner, a Kami/Bluespec/Verilog hardware development, the monograph, and the mathematical specification. The assumption receipt covers 13,100 statements across 446 files: 5,756 are closed under the global context, 7,344 depend on standard-library axioms, and none depend on project-local or third-party axioms. The standard-library dependencies use five named constants. Generic paid certification establishes accounting; semantic truth requires a sound checker. Hardware bridges retain their stated representation and compiler boundaries. The physical and foundational interpretations remain research questions.
